'''Ben Terrence Coates Jr.''' (born August 16, 1969) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[tight end]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 10 seasons, primarily with the [[New England Patriots]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Livingstone Blue Bears football|Livingstone Blue Bears]] and was selected by the Patriots in the fifth round of the [[1991 NFL draft]], where he spent all but one season of his NFL career. In his final season, he was a member of the [[Baltimore Ravens]].

During his nine seasons with the Patriots, Coates received five [[Pro Bowl]] and two first-team [[All-Pro]] selections. He also made an appearance in [[Super Bowl XXXI]]. After being released by the Patriots, Coates signed with the Ravens and was part of the team that won [[Super Bowl XXXV]]. Coates pursued a coaching career following his retirement, serving as the head coach at his alma mater Livingstone and the tight ends coach for the [[Cleveland Browns]]. He was named to the second [[National Football League 1990s All-Decade Team|NFL 1990s All-Decade Team]] in 2000 and inducted to the [[New England Patriots#Patriots Hall of Fame|New England Patriots Hall of Fame]] in 2008.

==Early life==
Coates was born on August 16, 1969, in [[Greenwood, South Carolina]], the youngest of eight children<ref name=":0">{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D3YOQcgupbc |title=NFL Legend Ben Coates opens up about career moments and untold life stories |date=2023-09-26 |last=ADSN TV |access-date=2025-07-25 |via=YouTube}}</ref> of Ben Coates Sr. and Mozella Coates. His oldest brother Gary Coates, was a significant influence, pushing him towards college and staying committed to working out and catching balls daily. Coates did not play football until his [[Senior (education)|senior]] year at [[Greenwood High School (South Carolina)|Greenwood High School]]. 
[[File:Ben Coates Livingstone College.jpg|thumb|Ben Coates, Livingstone College]]

At Livingstone, Coates became a multi-sport athlete, competing in both [[college football|football]] and [[college basketball|basketball]]. On the football field, he emerged as a dominant tight end, setting school records with 103 receptions for 1,268 yards and 18 touchdowns. He joined [[Phi Beta Sigma]] Fraternity, becoming a member through the Untouchable Upsilon Chapter on campus. Despite playing in the CIAA, a small-school [[NCAA Division II|Division II]] conference with limited national attention, Coates’s on-field production made him one of the top tight end prospects in the country. He was later inducted into the [[Central Intercollegiate Athletic Association]] (CIAA) Hall of Fame in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ben Coates (2018) - CIAA Hall of Fame Members |url=https://theciaa.com/hof.aspx?hof=281 |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=theciaa.com |language=en}}</ref>

==Professional career==

Considered an out-of-nowhere prospect, Coates was selected in the fifth round of the [[1991 NFL draft]] by the [[New England Patriots]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1991 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1991/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name="patriots">{{cite web|url=http://www.patriots.com/alumni/index.cfm?ac=alumnibiosdetail&bio=593|title=87 Ben Coates TE, Alumbi/bio detail|publisher=New England Patriots|access-date=February 2, 2010|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091114152700/http://www.patriots.com/alumni/index.cfm?ac=alumnibiosdetail&bio=593|archive-date=November 14, 2009}}</ref> His first two years with the Patriots were fairly uneventful; in his rookie year he had ten catches for 95 yards and a two-yard touchdown against the [[Indianapolis Colts]] that forced overtime in a 23–17 Patriots win. In his second season, he had 20 catches for 171 yards and three touchdowns.

His career changed with the 1993 arrival of [[quarterback]] [[Drew Bledsoe]] and [[head coach]] [[Bill Parcells]] to the Patriots franchise. Parcells, known for his reliance on tight ends, frequently used then-[[rookie]] quarterback Bledsoe on passes to Coates, and the tight end led the Patriots in receptions in 1993 with 53 catches for 629 yards and eight scores, two of them in New England's season-ending overtime win over [[1993 Miami Dolphins season|Miami]].

In 1994, his breakout year, he caught 96 passes, the most ever for a tight end to that point,<ref>{{cite web|last=Rank|first=Adam|url=http://www.nfl.com/photoessays/0ap2000000324888/NFL-players-from-historically-black-colleges|title=NFL players from historically black colleges|publisher=[[National Football League]]|date=February 10, 2014|access-date=February 27, 2014}}</ref> breaking a record previously set by [[Todd Christensen]] in 1986 (the record was later broken by [[Tony Gonzalez]] in 2004), for 1,174 yards receiving, the only time in his career he would gain 1,000 yards in a receiving season, while also scoring seven touchdowns. He appeared in his first of five consecutive [[Pro Bowl]]s.

In 1996, Coates had 62 catches for 682 yards and nine touchdowns; the most dramatic was against the [[New York Giants]] in the final game of the regular season as he caught a 12-yard pass and bulled through Giants defenders for the game-winning score of a 23–22 New England win. His efforts helped New England to a championship appearance in [[Super Bowl XXXI]]. His team lost the game, 35–21, but he had a good performance in it, leading the Patriots in receiving with 6 catches for 66 yards and a touchdown. From 1995 to 1998, he caught 84, 62, 66, and 67 passes, respectively, in those four seasons.

After the 1999 season, which saw a significant decline in production, Coates was released by the Patriots. He subsequently played for the [[Baltimore Ravens]], where he climbed the all-time receiving charts and won [[Super Bowl XXXV]] in the process. When Coates was released by the Ravens in the following year, he decided to retire, having become the fourth all-time leading receiver at tight end in NFL history, behind [[Ozzie Newsome]], former teammate [[Shannon Sharpe]], and [[Kellen Winslow]]. Coates played in 158 games with 499 receptions for 5,555 yards and 50 touchdowns.

After retiring, Coates returned to Livingstone College, where he was head coach, and also coached in [[NFL Europe]]. In 2004, he served an internship with the [[Dallas Cowboys]] as an assistant for the tight ends, reuniting him with head coach Parcells. In March 2005, Coates was named the tight ends coach for the [[Cleveland Browns]], replacing [[Rob Chudzinski]], under head coach [[Romeo Crennel]], who had been the defensive line coach of the Patriots while Coates was with the team.

It was announced on July 7, 2008, that Coates would be inducted into the [[New England Patriots#Patriots Hall of Fame|New England Patriots Hall of Fame]]. During his playing days with the Patriots, Coates was a fan favorite and was given the nickname "Winter" (as in "winter coat"), in addition to Ben "[[Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat|Technicolor Dream]]" Coates by [[ESPN]] commentator [[Chris Berman]].

==Coaching career==
===Livingstone College (2001–2004)===
After retiring from the NFL, Coates began his coaching career at [[Livingstone College]], his alma mater, serving as an offensive assistant from 2001 to 2004. During his tenure, he worked as the [[Position coach|offensive line coach]], quarterbacks coach, and wide receivers coach before becoming [[offensive coordinator]].

In 2004, he was invited to join the [[Dallas Cowboys]] as an assistant during training camp. Hand-picked by head coach [[Bill Parcells]], Coates assisted in the evaluation and development of the tight ends group.

===Frankfurt Galaxy (2004)===
Later in 2004, Coates joined the [[Frankfurt Galaxy (NFL Europe)|Frankfurt Galaxy]] of [[NFL Europe]] as an assistant offensive coach for tight ends. The team finished the season with a 7–3 record, placing second in the league, and went on to compete in [[World Bowl XII]].

===Cleveland Browns (2005–2007)===
From 2005 to 2007, Coates served as the tight ends coach for the [[Cleveland Browns]]. He managed the overall development of the tight end group and contributed to offensive game planning, scouting, and scripting. In 2006, under Coates’ coaching, tight end [[Kellen Winslow II]] recorded 89 receptions for 875 yards and 3 touchdowns — setting a franchise record for single-season receptions by a tight end and ranking 2nd in the NFL in tight end receptions, and 3rd in receiving yards by a tight end.

===Central State University (2009–2012)===
From 2009 to 2012, Coates served as the assistant head coach and offensive coordinator at [[Central State University]] in Ohio. In this role, he was responsible for implementing a comprehensive offensive system, supervising assistant coaches, and recruiting student-athletes.

===Saint Augustine’s University (2013–2014)===
Coates later worked as an assistant football coach at [[St. Augustine's University (North Carolina)|Saint Augustine’s University]] from 2013 to 2014, coaching wide receivers and supporting overall team development.

==Personal life==
Coates is the father of nine children: Lauren, Brianna, Bre'Yana, Gabriella, Brittany, Ben III, Anthony, Christopher, and Natasha. He has described his greatest accomplishment in life as "being able to see all my kids being able to see and make sure they all go to school so they can be successful in life." He has spoken publicly about the deep pride he feels watching his children grow and succeed, emphasizing education and [[moral character|character]] as his top priorities as a parent.

Two of his sons have followed in his athletic footsteps by playing college football at [[Livingstone College]], Coates’s [[alma mater]]. His son Ben Coates III plays [[tight end]], while his son Christopher Coates plays [[linebacker]]. Despite their athletic potential, Coates has stressed that education comes first, stating that the most important goal is for them to obtain their [[Academic degree|college degrees]], regardless of any future in professional sports.

Coates maintains a strong connection to his hometown of [[Greenwood, South Carolina]], and has continued to be involved in [[Mentorship|mentoring]] young athletes and supporting youth development both on and off the field.<ref name=":0" />

'''Barton Elliott "Barty" Smith''' (born March 23, 1952) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[fullback (gridiron football)|fullback]] for the [[Green Bay Packers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

==High school==
Born in [[Richmond, Virginia]], Smith graduated from [[Douglas S. Freeman High School]] where he was a four-sport star.  Smith was selected as the Virginia High School Player of the Year in 1969.  That same year he achieved the highest honor awarded to high school athletes when he was named to the Sunkist High School All-American Football Team.

==College career==
Smith played football for the [[Richmond Spiders football|University of Richmond]] where he was recognized as one of the nations best all-around fullbacks.  He starred in football at the University of Richmond from 1971 through 1973, twice being named to the All Southern Conference Football Team.  Recognized as one of the all time Spider greats, Smith led the University of Richmond to the Southern Conference Title and an appearance in the Tangerine Bowl.  He was the leader of the only Spider grid squad to be ranked in the Division 1 Top 20.
 
In 1972, Barty Smith was named as the recipient of the [[Jacobs Blocking Trophy]] presented to the Outstanding Blocker in the Southern Conference—an award which he repeated in 1973.  He became the fourth Richmond Spider to be honored since the award's inception in 1933.  In his senior year, Smith won the Coffman Award, representative of the Most Valuable Player in the East-West Shrine Game in San Francisco.  He ranks 8th on the University of Richmond's rushing list with 1,941 yards and career touchdowns with 15. 
 
In 1976, Smith was inducted into the University of Richmond Athletic Hall of Fame.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://vshfm.com/inductees/inductee_details.php?inducteeID=229 |title=Inductee Details - Virginia Sports Hall of Fame & Museum |access-date=2011-11-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120528211914/http://vshfm.com/inductees/inductee_details.php?inducteeID=229 |archive-date=2012-05-28 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 1990, he was named to the University of Richmond All-Time Football Team and was inducted into the Virginia High School Hall of Fame in 1998.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://vshfm.com/hall/induct_smithbarty.html |title=Class of 1999 : Barty Smith |publisher= Virginia Sports Hall of Fame |access-date=2011-11-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110816122408/http://vshfm.com/hall/induct_smithbarty.html |archive-date=2011-08-16 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Professional career==

After concluding a stellar career for the University of Richmond, Barty Smith was a first-round draft choice of the [[Green Bay Packers]] in 1974.  He played with Green Bay from 1974 until 1980.  Smith ranks 16th on the Packers all-time rushing list with 1,942 yards, scoring 18 career touchdowns.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/SmitBa00.htm|title=Barty Smith Stats|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com|access-date=1 November 2018}}</ref> He won Packer Offensive Player of the Year honors in 1977.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.packers.com/news-and-events/article_zeller/article-1/Smith-fondly-recalls-days-in-Green-Bay/f925b001-2b42-4fa6-8b3f-7d420490df93 |title=Smith fondly recalls days in Green Bay |access-date=2011-11-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607185518/http://www.packers.com/news-and-events/article_zeller/article-1/Smith-fondly-recalls-days-in-Green-Bay/f925b001-2b42-4fa6-8b3f-7d420490df93 |archive-date=2011-06-07 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

'''Beasley Young Reece Jr.''' (born March 18, 1954) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Dallas Cowboys]], [[New York Giants]] and [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[North Texas Mean Green football|North Texas State Mean Green]].

==Early life==
Reece attended [[La Vega High School]], where he played as a [[cornerback]]. He [[Walk-on (sports)|walked-on]] at [[North Texas State University]] in the spring of 1972.

The next year he played part-time. As a junior, he became a starter at left cornerback and had 2 interceptions. As a senior he posted 2 interceptions.

==Professional career==

===Dallas Cowboys===
Reece was selected by the [[Dallas Cowboys]] in the ninth round (264th overall) of the [[1976 NFL draft]]. The team drafted him as an athlete, so he spent his first weeks in [[Training camp (National Football League)|training camp]] as a [[cornerback]], before being switched to [[wide receiver]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1955&dat=19760823&id=_dshAAAAIBAJ&sjid=mqAFAAAAIBAJ&pg=1419,2531234 | title=Cowboy Changes | access-date=January 25, 2016}}</ref> Playing against the [[New Orleans Saints]]  in week 2, he registered his only [[NFL]] reception, which went for 6 yards, but also fumbled on the play.

The next year he requested the opportunity to compete at [[cornerback]]. He was waived on September 12, [[1977 NFL season|1977]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1298&dat=19770913&id=599NAAAAIBAJ&sjid=CosDAAAAIBAJ&pg=2360,1771813 | title=Transactions | access-date=January 25, 2016}}</ref>

===New York Giants===
On September 14, [[1977 NFL season|1977]], the [[New York Giants]] claimed him off waivers to play as a [[defensive back]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1893&dat=19770915&id=ZGwfAAAAIBAJ&sjid=L9UEAAAAIBAJ&pg=2562,1694865 | title=Transactions | access-date=January 25, 2016}}</ref> He became the starter at [[strong safety]] in [[1978 NFL season|1978]], before being switched to [[free safety]] in [[1981 NFL season|1981]].<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/08/01/sports/giants-find-reece-is-versatile-player.html | title=Giants Find Reece Is Versatile Player | work=The New York Times | date=August 1981 | access-date=January 25, 2016 | last1=Litsky | first1=Frank }}</ref>

In [[1983 NFL season|1983]], he asked for his release after rookie [[Terry Kinard]] was given the starting [[free safety]] position and he was cut on October 17.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/10/18/sports/giants-place-reece-on-the-waiver-list-club-agrees-to-request.html | title=Giants Place Reece On the Waiver List; Club Agrees To Request | work=The New York Times | date=18 October 1983 | access-date=January 25, 2016 | last1=Wallace | first1=William N. }}</ref>

===Tampa Bay Buccaneers===
The [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] claimed him off waivers on October 18, [[1983 NFL season|1983]].<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/10/19/sports/tampa-claims-reece.html | title=Tampa Claims Reece | work=The New York Times | date=19 October 1983 | access-date=January 25, 2016 | last1=Wallace | first1=William N. }}</ref> Despite playing only half of the season (8 starts), he registered 33 tackles, 5 passes defensed and led the team with 6 interceptions. The next year, he started 14 games at [[free safety]], finishing with 70 tackles, 12 passes defensed, one interception and 7 [[special teams]] tackles. He was waived on September 2, [[1985 NFL season|1985]].<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/09/03/sports/transactions-233952.html | title=Transactions | work=The New York Times | date=3 September 1985 | access-date=January 25, 2016}}</ref>

==Broadcasting career==
After his retirement from playing Reece worked as a [[color commentator]] and sideline reporter for NFL coverage on [[NFL on NBC|NBC]] and [[NFL on CBS|CBS]], and served as an analyst for the [[1992 Summer Olympics]] for NBC. During this time, he was the sports director for [[WVIT]] (NBC-30) in [[Hartford, Connecticut]]. He would also work in at [[WTOG]] [[Tampa Bay]]. When he came to CBS, he joined [[KYW-TV]] in [[Philadelphia]], and became their Sports Director, a position he held from July 1998 to July 2015. Reece is an [[Eagle Scout (Boy Scouts of America)|Eagle Scout]] and recipient of the [[Distinguished Eagle Scout Award]].<ref>{{cite web | last = Halter | first = Jon C. | date = Sep 2003 | url = http://www.scoutingmagazine.org/issues/0309/a-meet.html | title = Meeting in Philadelphia | work = Scouting Maganize | publisher = Boy Scouts of America | access-date = 2006-09-08| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20060828022735/http://www.scoutingmagazine.org/issues/0309/a-meet.html| archive-date= 28 August 2006 | url-status= live}}</ref><ref>[http://philadelphia.cbslocal.com/personality/beasley-reece/ Reece bio at cbsphilly.com] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101128100144/http://philadelphia.cbslocal.com/personality/beasley-reece/ |date=November 28, 2010 }} Retrieved 2010-12-19</ref>

In 2012, the Broadcast Pioneers of Philadelphia inducted Reece into its Hall of Fame.

On July 1, 2015, Reece was fired from KYW along with evening anchor Chris May and chief meteorologist [[Kathy Orr (meteorologist)|Kathy Orr]] as a new general manager decided to take the Eyewitness News program in a different direction.

==Personal life==
Reese and his wife Paula have been married since 1978. They have two children. Reese is an avid classical piano player and is a member of the [[Alpha Phi Alpha]] fraternity. He is a cousin of former [[NFL]] players [[Greg Pruitt]] and [[Randy Logan]].

'''Bartholomew Edward Scott''' (born August 18, 1980)<ref name="Scott PFR">{{cite web |title=Bart Scott |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/ScotBa20.htm |publisher=Pro Football Reference |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110813200125/http://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/ScotBa20.htm |archive-date=August 13, 2011 |access-date=December 27, 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> is an American sports analyst and former professional [[American football|football]] player. Scott was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for eleven seasons. After playing [[college football]] for the [[Southern Illinois Salukis football|Southern Illinois Salukis]], he was signed by the NFL's [[Baltimore Ravens]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2002. Scott was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]] in [[2007 Pro Bowl|2006]]. After playing his first seven years with the Ravens, Scott signed with the [[New York Jets]] in 2009. He would play his final four seasons for the Jets.<ref name="Lange, Randy">{{cite web |title=Five Are Gone, but 'They'll Always Be Jets' |url=http://blog.newyorkjets.com/2013/02/19/five-are-gone-but-theyll-always-be-jets/ |publisher=New York Jets |author=Lange, Randy |date=February 19, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130222065642/http://blog.newyorkjets.com/2013/02/19/five-are-gone-but-theyll-always-be-jets/ |archive-date=February 22, 2013 |access-date=February 19, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

He was employed as an NFL analyst for [[NFL on CBS|CBS]] television from 2013 to 2017. Scott is currently employed as the co-host of Bart and Carlin weekdays 10 to 1 on [[ESPN Radio]] in [[New York City]].

==Early life==

Scott attended [[Southeastern High School (Detroit, Michigan)|Southeastern High School]] in Detroit, coached by Drake Wilkins, where he played running back and linebacker on the football team.<ref name="Scott, SI"/> Scott's assistant coach, Reinard Davis, recalled that "[Scott] went 110 percent on every snap and never came off the field."<ref name="Scott, SI">{{cite magazine |title=Bart Scott (53) |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2007/writers/tim_layden/08/28/scott0903/index.html |magazine=Sports Illustrated |author=Layden, Tim |date=August 28, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111211164749/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2007/writers/tim_layden/08/28/scott0903/index.html |archive-date=December 11, 2011 |access-date=December 27, 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> During his senior year, Scott recorded 76 tackles and led the team in rushing with 635 yards.<ref name="Scott, BR">{{cite web |title=Big Year for Bart |url=http://preview.baltimoreravens.com/News/Articles/2008/05/Big_Year_for_Bart.aspx |publisher=Baltimore Ravens |author=Duffy, Mike |date=May 22, 2008 |archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/5vIT6P5vG?url=http://preview.baltimoreravens.com/News/Articles/2008/05/Big_Year_for_Bart.aspx |archive-date=December 27, 2010 |access-date=December 27, 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

More than one hundred colleges sent recruiting letters; however, low [[SAT]] scores made colleges wary of offering Scott a scholarship.<ref name="Scott, SI"/> Scott later improved his test scores to ensure eligibility.<ref name="Scott, SI"/> During July workouts for a Michigan high school all-star game, Scott was impressive on the field, catching the interest of coach Bryan Masi. Masi contacted Dan Enos, a friend and an assistant coach at [[Southern Illinois University|Southern Illinois]]; the Southern Illinois staff decided to offer Scott a scholarship.<ref name="Scott, SI"/>

Scott continues to return to Southeastern High School nearly every year to speak with students.<ref name="Scott, BR"/> Additionally, Scott paid for new uniforms and equipment in 2005 and provided money to upgrade the weight room in 2007.<ref name="Scott, BR"/> Scott also paid to have a new set of bleachers installed at the school after vandals stole the school's former bleachers.<ref>{{cite news |title=Bart Scott pays for new bleachers at his high school after theft |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/blogs/jets/2010/10/bart-scott-pays-for-new-bleach.html |work=New York Daily News |author=Mehta, Manish |date=October 5, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101009133714/http://www.nydailynews.com/blogs/jets/2010/10/bart-scott-pays-for-new-bleach.html |archive-date=October 9, 2010 |access-date=December 27, 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In honor of Scott's accomplishments on and off the field, Southeastern retired his jersey in 2008.<ref name="Scott, BR"/>

==College career==

At [[Southern Illinois University]], Scott played linebacker and safety for the [[Southern Illinois Salukis football]] team. As a junior, Scott was suspended from the team for the final six games of the season following an altercation with defensive coordinator Michael Vite who chastised Scott for eating during a locker room meeting.<ref name="Scott, SI"/> At the end of the year, the team's entire coaching staff was fired; [[Jerry Kill]] was hired as the new head coach.<ref name="Scott, SI"/> Kill had been warned by a former staff members about Scott's behavior. However, Kill was impressed by Scott, calling him "a captain and leader."<ref name="Scott, SI"/> During his senior year, Scott led the team with 127 tackles and 5.5 sacks; earning first-team All-Gateway conference honors.<ref name="Scott, BR"/>

Kill touted Scott's abilities to several NFL teams but only the [[Baltimore Ravens]] sent out a scout to assess Scott.<ref name="Scott, SI"/> The scout was impressed by Scott and three days following the [[2002 NFL draft]], after going [[undrafted]], Scott signed a contract with the Ravens.<ref name="Scott, SI"/>

Scott later returned to Southern Illinois in 2005 to finish his academic studies, graduating with a degree in economics.<ref name="Scott Bio">{{cite web |title=Bart Scott |url=http://www.newyorkjets.com/team/roster/Bart-Scott/2942b6ed-627d-49bf-a7a4-2b0f06c7fbb7 |publisher=New York Jets |year=2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101228153538/http://www.newyorkjets.com/team/roster/Bart-Scott/2942b6ed-627d-49bf-a7a4-2b0f06c7fbb7 |archive-date=December 28, 2010 |access-date=December 27, 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Scott later became a first-ballot member of the Southern Illinois Hall of Fame.<ref name="Scott, BR"/>

==Professional career==
===Baltimore Ravens===
During Scott's first three years with Baltimore, he was a special teams standout. However, he saw little time in the defensive rotation.<ref name="Scott, SI"/><ref name="Baltimore Ties">{{cite news |title=Scott, Star in New York With Jets, Can't Put Ties to Baltimore Aside |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/10/sports/football/10jets.html?_r=1 |work=The New York Times |author=Bishop, Greg |date=September 9, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180901080718/https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/10/sports/football/10jets.html?_r=1 |archive-date=September 1, 2018 |access-date=December 27, 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In his [[2002 NFL season|rookie season]], he played in all 16 regular season games and recorded five tackles and one interception on defense while tying with another teammate to lead the team in special teams tackles at 17.<ref name="Scott Bio"/> He made his NFL debut at the [[Carolina Panthers]] on September 8, 2002.<ref name="Scott Bio"/> The following season, he again played in all 16 games and one post-season game, recording nine tackles and one fumble recovery on defense.<ref name="Scott Bio"/> His 19 special teams tackles, a career high, ranked second on the team.<ref name="Scott Bio"/> In the [[2004 NFL season|2004 season]], he played in 13 games, making 17 special teams tackles, adding five tackles on defense playing as a safety and linebacker.<ref name="Scott Bio"/>
[[File:Michael Vick passing, November 2006.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Scott (57) and [[Michael Vick]] in 2006]]
[[File:BartScott.jpg|thumbnail|right|Scott as a member of the [[Baltimore Ravens]]]]

Scott saw significant playing time during the [[2005 NFL season|2005 season]] as [[Ray Lewis (American football)|Ray Lewis]] suffered a [[hamstring]] injury,<ref name="Scott, SI"/> playing in all 16 games and making 10 starts.<ref name="Scott Bio"/> He finished the season with 119 tackles, four sacks, two forced fumbles, one fumble recovery and four passes defended.<ref name="Scott Bio"/> Scott signed a three-year, $13.5 million contract extension with the Ravens, turning down an offer from the [[Cleveland Browns]].<ref name="Scott, SI"/> In 2006, Scott ended the season with a career-high 135 tackles, 9.5 sacks, two interceptions and nine passes defended.<ref name="Scott Bio"/> He played in the [[2007 Pro Bowl|Pro Bowl]] in Hawaii as an alternate after being elected to replace his teammate Ray Lewis.<ref name="Scott Bio"/> Scott was named to the [[Associated Press]]' second All-Pro team.<ref name="Scott Bio"/>

Scott started all 16 games for the second straight season and recorded 131 tackles, one sack and three passes defended.<ref name="Scott Bio"/> On December 3, 2007, Scott was penalized twice for [[unsportsmanlike conduct]] in the fourth quarter of the [[Monday Night Football]] game against the [[New England Patriots]]. The second call came after Scott picked up the official's flag from the first call and threw it. Following the game, teammate [[Samari Rolle]] made accusations of disrespectful language by the official involved.<ref>{{cite web |title=Rolle accuses official of using disrespectful language |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3141124 |publisher=ESPN |date=December 4, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121022165605/http://sports.espn.go.com/nfl/news/story?id=3141124 |archive-date=October 22, 2012 |access-date=December 27, 2010 |url-status=live }}</ref> In his final year with Baltimore, Scott again started all 16 games contributing with 104 tackles, 1.5 sacks and five passes defended.<ref name="Scott Bio"/>

===New York Jets===
[[File:Bart Scott.JPG|thumb|150px|right|Scott during a 2009 Jets training camp session]]
In 2009, Scott became a free agent. Both the Ravens and [[New York Jets]] vied for Scott's services.<ref name="Scott, Jets">{{cite web |title=Scott picks Jets over Ravens |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3940727 |publisher=ESPN |date=February 28, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110511105202/http://sports.espn.go.com/nfl/news/story?id=3940727 |archive-date=May 11, 2011 |access-date=December 27, 2010 |url-status=live }}</ref> After the Jets amended their contract offer by adding a year to the deal, Scott signed the six-year, $48 million contract with New York on February 27, 2009. This reunited him with head coach [[Rex Ryan]], his former defensive coach in Baltimore, whom Scott has stated he would follow anywhere.<ref name="Baltimore Ties"/><ref name="Scott, Jets"/>

Scott started every game in his first season with New York, finishing the year with 92 tackles and a sack.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bart Scott 2009 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/ScotBa20/gamelog/2009/ |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

After the Jets defeated the [[New England Patriots]] in an AFC Divisional Playoff game on January 16, 2011, [[ESPN]]'s [[Sal Paolantonio]] approached Scott for an interview. Scott interrupted Paolantonio with a rant supporting his team and antagonizing "non-believers", specifically calling out [[ESPN]]'s [[Tom Jackson (American football, born 1951)|Tom Jackson]]. A clip of the interview went [[viral video|viral]] after being posted on [[YouTube]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Scott interview becoming legendary|url=https://www.espn.com/new-york/nfl/columns/story?columnist=howard_johnette&id=6038901|publisher=ESPN|author=Howard, Johnette|date=January 21, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120512124722/http://sports.espn.go.com/new-york/nfl/columns/story?columnist=howard_johnette&id=6038901|archive-date=May 12, 2012|access-date=January 6, 2012|url-status=live}}</ref> Despite Scott's boasting, the Jets lost to the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] in the AFC Championship the following week. On March 3, 2011, Scott made an appearance for professional wrestling promotion [[Total Nonstop Action Wrestling]] (TNA) on their ''[[TNA Impact!]]'' television show, appearing alongside [[Hulk Hogan]] and [[Ric Flair]] at a wedding ceremony between [[Jeff Jarrett]] and [[Karen Jarrett]] and in the end tapping out to [[Kurt Angle]]'s [[Professional wrestling holds#Ankle lock|ankle lock]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Caldwell's TNA Impact report 3/3: Ongoing "virtual-time" coverage of Impact on Spike TV - Hogan, wedding, 3/3/11 reveal, Tag Title match, retirement match, celebrities |url=http://pwtorch.com/artman2/publish/tnaimpact/article_48210.shtml |publisher=Pro Wrestling Torch |author=Caldwell, James |date=March 3, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111116164819/http://pwtorch.com/artman2/publish/tnaimpact/article_48210.shtml |archive-date=November 16, 2011 |access-date=March 4, 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Scott's final two years with the Jets were marred by struggles and controversy on and off the field. On January 1, 2012, the day after the Jets missed the playoffs after losing their last 3 games, Scott was fined $10,000 for showing an obscene gesture in front of a cameraman while in the locker room.<ref>{{cite news |title=Bart Scott's middle finger gesture at photographer in NY Jets locker room will be investigated by NFL |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/jets/nfl-investigate-ny-jet-bart-scott-obscene-gesture-article-1.1000597 |work=New York Daily News |author=Mehta, Manish |date=January 3, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140323005410/http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/jets/nfl-investigate-ny-jet-bart-scott-obscene-gesture-article-1.1000597 |archive-date=March 23, 2014 |access-date=April 29, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> That September, Scott threatened to assault a photographer in the Jets' locker room.<ref>{{cite news |title=NY Jets' Bart Scott threatens to 'smack the s---' out of a reporter trying to take his picture in locker room |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/jets/ny-jets-bart-scott-threatens-smack-s-reporter-picture-locker-room-article-1.1164849 |work=New York Daily News |author=Walder, Seth |date=September 21, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140109035111/http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/jets/ny-jets-bart-scott-threatens-smack-s-reporter-picture-locker-room-article-1.1164849 |archive-date=January 9, 2014 |access-date=April 29, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In November, Scott tried and failed to organize a media boycott; however, it lasted only a few moments.<ref>{{cite news|last=Armstrong|first=Kevin|title=Bart Scott's media boycott fails as safety Yeramiah Bell breaks mutiny|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/jets/jets-insider-bart-media-boycott-fails-article-1.1204221|location=New York|work=Daily News|date=November 19, 2012}}</ref> Later that month, Scott verbally attacked fans after the Jets gave up 35 second quarter points in a 49–19 blowout loss to New England.<ref>{{cite news|last=Mehta|first=Manish|title=Bart Scott rips Jets fans|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/blogs/jets/2012/11/bart-scott-rips-jets-fans-for-heckling-players-on-thanksgiving-night|work=New York Daily News}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://newyork.cbslocal.com/2012/11/29/bart-scott-calls-out-jets-fans-craig-carton-challenges-linebacker-to-dodgeball-game/ |publisher=CBS New York |title=Bart Scott Calls Out Jets Fans; Craig Carton Challenges Linebacker To Dodgeball Game |date=November 29, 2012 |access-date=July 9, 2013}}</ref> The Jets failed to make the playoffs in Scott's final two seasons with the team putting up a combined record of 14–18. According to [[Pro Football Focus]], Scott ranked last among inside linebackers in tackling efficiency in 2012.<ref>{{cite news |title=The Sharp Decline of Bart Scott |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424127887323330604578141411224614532 |work=The Wall Street Journal |author=Sielski, Mike |date=November 25, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121127214203/http://online.wsj.com/article/SB10001424127887323330604578141411224614532.html |archive-date=November 27, 2012 |access-date=April 29, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The Jets released Scott on February 19, 2013.<ref name="Lange, Randy"/>

==Broadcasting career==
===Television career===
After drawing some interest from teams during the off-season, Scott retired and was hired by [[CBS Sports]] as an analyst for [[CBS Sports Network]]'s ''That Other Pregame Show''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/9588454/ex-baltimore-ravens-new-york-jets-lb-bart-scott-joins-cbs-sports|title=Ex-Ravens, Jets LB Scott joins CBS Sports|date=August 21, 2013 }}</ref>

In February 2014, it was announced that Scott would join CBS' ''[[The NFL Today]]'' for the 2014 season.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cbssports.com/nfl/eye-on-football/24455524/bart-scott-joins-cbs-sports-the-nfl-today-in-2014|title=Bart Scott joins CBS Sports' 'The NFL Today' in 2014|last=Wilson|first=Ryan|publisher=CBSSports.com|date=February 24, 2014|access-date=March 4, 2014}}</ref> In 2017, it was announced that Scott was replaced by [[Nate Burleson]].

In December 2021, Scott advocated for the Baltimore Ravens to injure [[Joe Burrow]] in future games after they lost to the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] 41–21. While speaking on ESPN's "[[Get Up (TV program)|Get Up]]", he said in reference to Burrow, "He's gonna get the rib shot. He's gonna get the neck shot. He's going to get the tackle the arms, bust his head off the ground shot" and also that the Ravens had put a "red dot" on him.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Roling |first=Chris |date=2021-12-30 |title=Best reactions to Bart Scott saying Ravens have a 'red dot' on Joe Burrow |url=https://bengalswire.usatoday.com/lists/bart-scott-ravens-red-dot-joe-burrow-best-reactions/ |access-date=2023-01-03 |website=Bengals Wire|publisher=USA Today |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |title=Reacting to Joe Burrow's 525-yard performance 🤯{{!}} Get Up | date=December 30, 2021 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yCatct2bAUs |language=en |access-date=2023-01-03}}</ref>

===Radio career===
In November 2017, Scott was named as the replacement, along with Chris Carlin and Maggie Gray, for long-time [[WFAN (AM)|WFAN]] host [[Mike Francesa]] during the afternoon drive. In January 2020, alongside [[Alan Hahn]], Scott launched a local show for [[ESPN New York]] in the mid-day slot previously occupied by [[Stephen A. Smith]].

==Personal life==
{| class="toccolours" style="float: right; margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 2em; font-size: 85%; background:#c6dbf7; color:black; width:30em; max-width: 40%;" cellspacing="5"
| style="text-align: left;" | "I wasn't supposed to make it out of Detroit. I wasn't supposed to get a scholarship. I was supposed to be [covering] kicks the rest of my life. But here I am. I'm a man playing with the house's money, and that's a dangerous man."<ref name="Scott, SI"/>
|-
| style="text-align: left;" | — Bart Scott

Scott grew up relatively poor in the violence-filled and drug-infested neighborhood of Hurlbut Street on the east side of Detroit.<ref name="Scott, SI"/><ref name="Scott, NYT">{{Citation |title=The Jets' Bart Scott, a Warrior Shaped by Women |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/23/sports/football/23jets.html |work=The New York Times |author=Bishop, Greg |date=April 22, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170930120804/http://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/23/sports/football/23jets.html?_r=1 |archive-date=September 30, 2017 |access-date=December 27, 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In spite of this, Scott received guidance from multiple sources including his parents, Dorita Adams and Bart Capers and other family members.<ref name="Scott, SI"/><ref name="Scott, NYT"/>

Scott has been very involved with the community; he is involved in multiple charities,<ref name="Scott, SI"/><ref name="Scott, BR"/><ref name="Scott, NYT"/> including A Son Never Forgets, a foundation dedicated to helping those suffering with paralysis which was established by Scott himself in October 2006.<ref name="Scott, BR"/><ref name="Scott Bio"/> Scott has also dedicated money to his former neighborhood, buying a plot of land to build a playground near his grandmother's home<ref name="Scott, SI"/><ref name="Scott, NYT"/> in addition to providing equipment and speaking with students at his alma mater, [[Southeastern High School (Detroit, Michigan)|Southeastern High School]].<ref name="Scott, BR"/>

Scott is married to Darnesha. They have three children, two sons and a daughter.<ref name="Scott, BR"/><ref name="Scott Bio"/> Because of the concussion issue, Scott expressed at one time that he did not want his son to play football.<ref>{{Citation|title=NY Jets linebacker Bart Scott does not want son to play football as NFL continues to battle with concussion issue|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/jets/ny-jets-linebacker-bart-scott-son-play-football-nfl-continues-battle-concussion-issue-article-1.1085074|work=Daily News|author=Myers, Gary|date=May 26, 2012|access-date=January 1, 2014|location=New York}}</ref>

'''Barry Quentin Word''' (born January 17, 1964), nicknamed "'''the Last Word'''",<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-11-02-sp-3756-story.html | title=They Are Willing to Be Patient : Barry Word: He had 200 yards in one game, but is No. 2 in a one-back offense. | work=[[Los Angeles Times]] | date=Nov 2, 1990 | accessdate=20 March 2026 | author=Baker, Chris}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-olympian/193813359/ | title=In K.C., Word up means big gain | work=[[The Olympian]] | date=October 18, 1990 | accessdate=20 March 2026 | author=Wood, Gail | pages=B4}}</ref> is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

==Early life==
Barry Quentin Word was born on January 17, 1964, in [[Long Island, Virginia]].<ref name="pfr"/> He attended [[Halifax County High School]] in [[South Boston, Virginia]].<ref name="pfr">{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WordBa00.htm | title=Barry Word | publisher=[[Pro Football Reference]] | accessdate=20 March 2026}}</ref>

==College career==
Word played [[college football]] at the [[University of Virginia]]. In 1985, he ran for 1224 yards, which is currently the fifth most rushing yards total put up by a [[Virginia Cavaliers]] running back. Also in 1985, Word was the [[Atlantic Coast Conference]] player of the year.

==Professional career==
Barry Word was selected in the third round, 62nd overall, by the [[New Orleans Saints]] in the [[1986 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1986 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1986/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-02 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Shortly after being drafted, he and two other Virginia athletes were indicted on cocaine distribution charges. The Saints did not offer a contract to Word after his indictment but retained his football rights.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1987-05-03-sp-8532-story.html | title=Barry Word, Now Getting 2nd Chance, Trying to be a Saint | website=[[Los Angeles Times]] | date=3 May 1987 }}</ref> Word pleaded guilty, but his willingness to cooperate and his limited involvement in the case meant he only received 5 months in prison.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/07/30/sports/sports-people-virginia-star-pleads.html|title=SPORTS PEOPLE; Virginia Star Pleads|date=July 30, 1986|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=2009-10-03}}</ref> After Word's release from prison in March 1987, he signed a three-year contract with the Saints and ran for 133 yards as a [[Halfback (American football)|halfback]] in his rookie year. In 1988, however, he fell to third-string running back for the Saints behind [[Rueben Mayes]] and [[Dalton Hilliard]], two running backs drafted by the Saints the prior year. Unhappy with being shifted from running back to halfback, Word walked away from the Saints after two games in 1988. He then had unsuccessful attempts to join the Dallas Cowboys later in 1988 and with the Pittsburgh Steelers in 1989.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1990/10/16/word-full-speed-ahead-in-drive-to-succeed/3fc8ec4a-a79e-4197-8fae-a3da48186ead/ |title=WORD FULL SPEED AHEAD IN DRIVE TO SUCCEED |date=1990-10-16 |author1=Alan Eskew |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |place=Washington, D.C. |issn=0190-8286 |oclc=1330888409}}</ref> He was finally signed by the Kansas City Chiefs before the start of the 1990 season.

Word had a career year in 1990, rushing for 1015 yards on 204 carries, garnering [[NFL Comeback Player of the Year Award]] for his performance. He split carries with [[Christian Okoye]] during the 1990 season as well as the next two years. At the start of the 1994 season Word was traded to the Minnesota Vikings and he ran for 847 yards on 142 carries. He was signed by the Cardinals at the start of the 1994 season, but only played one game for them and did not have a rushing attempt. This was to be the last time he took the field in the NFL as he retired after the game. He has said that being able to retire early is not a bad thing, and said as much to [[Tiki Barber]] when Barber was set to retire concluding the 2006 season.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.phillyburbs.com/pb-dyn/news/99-12142006-755193.html |title=Barber has no regrets about hanging them up |access-date=2007-01-01 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081202105140/http://www.phillyburbs.com/pb-dyn/news/99-12142006-755193.html |archive-date=2008-12-02 }}</ref>

Head coach | highlights = * [[Arena Football League|AFL]] MVP (1988) * 3× First-team All-Arena ([[1988 All-Arena Team|1988]], [[1993 All-Arena Team|1993]], [[1994 All-Arena Team|1994]]) * Second-team All-Arena ([[1990 All-Arena Team|1990]]) * [[Arena Football Hall of Fame|AFL Hall of Fame]] (2000) * AFL 25 Greatest Players – #23 (2012) * Third-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] ([[1983 College Football All-America Team|1983]]) * 2× [[Atlantic Coast Conference|ACC]] [[Player of the Year]] (1982, 1983) * 2× First-team [[List of All-Atlantic Coast Conference football teams|All-ACC]] ([[1982 All-Atlantic Coast Conference football team|1982]], [[1983 All-Atlantic Coast Conference football team|1983]]) * [[Atlantic Coast Conference|ACC]] Rookie of the Year (1980) | statlabel1 = Completions | statvalue1 = 2 | statlabel2 = Attempts | statvalue2 = 5 | statlabel3 = Passing yards | statvalue3 = 25 | statlabel4 = [[Touchdown|TD]]–[[Interception|INT]] | statvalue4 = 0–1 | aflstatlabel1 = Attempts-Completions | aflstatvalue1 = 1,928-1,069 | aflstatlabel2 = Passing yards | aflstatvalue2 = 14,168 | aflstatlabel3 = TD–INT | aflstatvalue3 = 267–81 | pfr = BennBe20 | afl = 113 }} '''Allen Beverly''' "'''Ben'''" '''Bennett II''' (born May 5, 1962) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Dallas Cowboys]], [[Cincinnati Bengals]] and [[Chicago Bears]]. He also was a member of the [[Jacksonville Bulls]], [[Chicago Bruisers]], [[Dallas Texans (Arena)|Dallas Texans]], [[Sacramento Surge]], [[San Antonio Riders]], [[Orlando Predators]], [[San Jose SaberCats]] and [[Portland Forest Dragons]]. He was a football coach in the [[Arena Football League]] (AFL), [[af2]], and [[National Arena League]] (NAL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Duke Blue Devils football|Duke Blue Devils]], earning third team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors in 1983. ==Early life== Bennett attended [[Peterson High School]] in [[Sunnyvale, California]], where he was the starter at [[quarterback]].{{cite web| url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2013/09/02/santa-clara-valley-is-and-has-always-been-a-hotbed-for-qbs/ | title=Santa Clara Valley is–and has always been–a hotbed for QBs | date=September 2, 2013 | access-date=January 27, 2019}} He was the [[team captain]] and a highly recruited player as a senior. In his high school career he set 18 school records and 9 [[Santa Clara Valley Athletic League]] records. ==College career== ===Freshman season=== Bennett accepted a football scholarship from [[Duke University]] under then-head coach [[Shirley Wilson|Shirley "Red" Wilson]] and [[offensive coordinator]] [[Steve Spurrier]].{{Cite web |date=April 19, 2012 |title=Former Preds QB looks to make impact as offensive coordinator |url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2012/04/19/former-preds-qb-looks-to-make-impact-as-offensive-coordinator/ |access-date=January 27, 2019 |website=Orlando Sentinel}} He was voted ACC "Rookie of the Year" and twice named the ACC "Offensive Player of the Week". His best individual game was against [[Wake Forest University]], setting three NCAA freshman records by completing 38 of 62 passes for 469 yards. He finished the season with 174 of 330 completions for 2,050 yards, 11 touchdowns and a school record 25 interceptions.{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/11/09/sports/bennett-is-spark-at-duke.html | title=Bennett is Spark at Duke | newspaper=The New York Times | date=November 9, 1982 | access-date=January 27, 2019}} ===Sophomore season=== In [[1981 Duke Blue Devils football team|1981]], he injured his shoulder during the season opener, missing the next three games and he also had to overcome a challenge for the starting job from backup Ron Sally. He [[Punt (gridiron football)|punted]] against the [[University of South Carolina]] twice for an average of 41 yards. He came back against [[Virginia Tech Hokies football|Virginia Tech]] and completed 9 of 16 passes for 113 yards with one touchdown. He had his best games against [[Maryland Terrapins football|Maryland]] (31 of 46 for 397 yards and 2 touchdowns) and [[Clemson University]] (17 of 25 for 243 yards and one touchdown). In nine games, he completed 110 of 202 passes for 1,445 yards, with 7 touchdowns and 8 interceptions. ===Junior season=== In [[1982 Duke Blue Devils football team|1982]], he became the first player in the ACC in its 30 years history to pass for over 3,000 yards with 3,033, receiving ACC [[Player of the Year]] and [[Atlantic Coast Conference|All-ACC]] honors. He set numerous records, including ACC career marks for most passing yards (6,528), most passes attempted (906), most passes completed (520), and most touchdown passes (38). He was named ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'''s Offensive Player of the Week following the season finale against [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill|University of North Carolina]] while passing for 273 yards, completing 25 of 34 passes, with one touchdown and no interceptions. In the 4th quarter against [[Navy Midshipmen football|Navy]], he completed an NCAA record 21 passes with three touchdowns. He threw at least one touchdown pass in every game. Bennett had a completion percentage of 63.1 and a [[Passer rating|passing efficiency rating]] of 142.5. In 11 games, he completed 236 of 374 attempts for 3,033 yards with 20 touchdowns and 12 interceptions.{{cite web | url=http://www.goduke.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=4200&ATCLID=205435980 | title=Ben Bennett Hall of Fame Bio | access-date=January 27, 2019 | archive-date=August 6, 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180806084920/http://www.goduke.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=4200&ATCLID=205435980 | url-status=dead }} ===Senior season=== In [[1983 Duke Blue Devils football team|1983]], he completed 300 of 469 pass attempts for 3,086 yards with 17 touchdowns and one interception, averaging 280.54 yards per game.{{cite web| url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1983/11/22/Duke-quarterback-Ben-Bennett-the-all-time-leading-passer-in/3798438325200/ | title=Duke quarterback Ben Bennett, the all-time leading passer in... | access-date=January 27, 2019}} Bennett completed his [[College football|collegiate career]] as the top passer in the history of [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] [[Division I-A]] football, with the most passes attempted (1,375), most passes completed (820), and most yardage (9,614), surpassing marks set by [[John Elway]] and [[Jim McMahon]]. He left with 7 [[NCAA]], 15 [[Atlantic Coast Conference|ACC]] and 42 school records. In 2011, he was inducted into the [[Duke University]] Athletics Hall of Fame. In 2011, he was a member of the ACC Legends Class.{{cite web| url=http://www.goduke.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=4200&ATCLID=205240658 | title=Bennett Named to 2011 ACC Legends Class | date=August 9, 2011 | access-date=January 27, 2019}} ==Professional career== Bennett was selected by the [[Atlanta Falcons]] in the 6th round (148th overall) of the [[1984 NFL draft]].{{Cite web |title=1984 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1984/draft.htm |access-date=October 12, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}{{cite web| url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1984/05/02/Atlanta-Falcons-coach-Dan-Henning-said-he-didnt-plan/1255452318400/ | title=The Atlanta Falcons Monday waived six players, including former... | access-date=January 27, 2019}} On May 5, he instead chose to sign with the [[Jacksonville Bulls]] of the [[United States Football League]], who selected him in the [[USFL Territorial Draft|1984 territorial draft]].{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/01/30/sports/flutie-and-bennett-a-contrast.html | title=Flutie and Bennett, a Contrast | newspaper=The New York Times | date=January 30, 1985 | access-date=January 27, 2019| last1=Wallace | first1=William N. }} He was a backup behind [[Robbie Mahfouz]] and [[Matt Robinson (American football)|Matt Robinson]]. He appeared in 2 games, completing 7 of 13 passes for 113 yards with one touchdown and no interceptions. On February 7, [[1985 USFL season|1985]], he was released after the signing of [[Brian Sipe]].{{cite web| url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/02/27/Brian-Sipe-was-in-satisfactory-condition-after-surgery-to/2805478328400/ | title=Brian Sipe was in satisfactory condition after surgery to... | access-date=January 27, 2019}} On February 26, [[1985 NFL season|1985]], he was signed by the Falcons to participate in their [[National Football League Training Camp|training camp]].{{cite web| url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/03/01/Former-Georgia-center-Wayne-Radloff-who-spent-the-last/2332478501200/ | title=Former Georgia center Wayne Radloff, who spent the last... | access-date=January 27, 2019}} He was waived on August 4.{{cite web| url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/08/05/The-Atlanta-Falcons-Monday-waived-six-players-including-former/9864492062400/ | title=Atlanta Falcons coach Dan Henning said he didn't plan... | access-date=January 27, 2019}} In [[1986 NFL season|1986]], he signed as a [[free agent]] with the [[Houston Oilers]]. He was cut on August 25.{{cite news| url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1986/08/26/nfl-preseason/09829b02-9aad-4207-b173-d7834d996d62/ | title=Transactions | newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] | access-date=January 27, 2019}} After the [[NFLPA]] strike was declared on the third week of the [[1987 NFL season|1987 season]], those contests were canceled (reducing the 16-game season to 15) and the [[NFL]] decided that the games would be played with replacement players. He was signed to be a part of the Dallas replacement team that was given the mock name "Rhinestone Cowboys" by the media on October 1.{{cite news|title=Who's playing today and for whom|newspaper=Lakeland Ledger|date=October 4, 1987}} He was a backup [[quarterback]] and didn't appear in any game. He was cut on October 7. On October 9, he was claimed off waivers by the [[Cincinnati Bengals]]. He played in one game, completing 2 of 6 passes for 25 yards with one interception. He wasn't re-signed after the season. In [[1988 Arena Football League season|1988]], he was signed by the [[Chicago Bruisers]] of the [[Arena Football League]] after performing well at a tryout camp.{{cite web| url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1994/05/19/preds-quarterback-pulling-double-duty/ | title=Preds' Quarterback Pulling Double Duty | date=May 19, 1994 | access-date=January 27, 2019}} Under head coach [[Perry Moss]], he finished the season completing 172 of 323 passes for 2,304 yards with 49 touchdowns and 13 interceptions. He was named First-team All-Arena team at QB and was also named the league's Most Valuable Player. On November 29, [[1988 NFL season|1988]], he was signed as a [[free agent]] by the [[Chicago Bears]] to backup [[Jim Harbaugh]], after [[Jim McMahon]] was placed on the [[injured reserve list]] and [[Mike Tomczak]] was out with a separated shoulder.{{cite news| url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1988/11/30/notebook/e16f681c-f0fb-4a9a-a73a-58f2b679b0c8/ | title=Transactions | newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] | access-date=January 27, 2019}} He was active for two games as a backup [[quarterback]]. He wasn't re-signed after the season. In [[1989 Arena Football League season|1989]], the Bruisers suspended operations. During the shortened season, he was the league's top-ranked passer, posting 69 of 127 completions for 808 yards with 14 touchdowns and 5 interceptions. In [[1990 Arena Football League season|1990]], Bennett began the year with the [[Indiana Firebirds|Albany Firebirds]]. On May 14, he was traded to the [[Dallas Texans (Arena)|Dallas Texans]].{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1957&dat=19900621&id=GXMhAAAAIBAJ&sjid=tIgFAAAAIBAJ&pg=2823,5235945 |title=Preseason Deal Could Come Back to Haunt Firebirds |author=Tom Boggie |date=June 21, 1990 |newspaper=The Daily Gazette |access-date=October 31, 2013}} He appeared in all 8 games where he led the team to the [[ArenaBowl IV]]. During the season, he completed 115 of 220 attempts for 1,149 yards, 24 touchdowns, and 15 interceptions. He was named second-team All-Arena. In [[1991 WLAF season|1991]], he was selected by the [[Sacramento Surge]] in the first round of the [[World League of American Football]] draft.{{cite web| url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1991-02-19-9101160503-story.html | title=New League Picks QBs with a Lot of Mileage | website=[[Chicago Tribune]] | date=February 19, 1991 | access-date=January 27, 2019}} He was a backup behind [[Mike Elkins]] and was released on April 9.{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/04/10/sports/transactions-928191.html | title=Transactions | newspaper=The New York Times | date=April 10, 1991 | access-date=January 27, 2019}} In April, he was signed by the [[San Antonio Riders]], where he was a backup behind [[Mike Johnson (American football coach)|Mike Johnson]] and [[Jason Garrett]]. On June 5, [[1991 Arena Football League season|1991]], he was signed by the [[Dallas Texans (Arena)|Dallas Texans]] of the [[Arena Football League]].{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/06/06/sports/transactions-917691.html | title=Transactions | newspaper=The New York Times | date=June 6, 1991 | access-date=January 27, 2019}} On July 3, he was traded to the expansion [[Orlando Predators]] in exchange for [[defensive tackle]] Keith Williams, reuniting with head coach [[Perry Moss]].{{cite web| url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1991/07/04/predators-acquire-bennett-williams/ | title=Predators Acquire Bennett, Williams | date=July 4, 1991 | access-date=January 27, 2019}} He replaced starter [[Reggie Collier]], finishing the season with 42 of 81 passes for 540 yards with 6 touchdowns and 2 interceptions. In [[1992 Arena Football League season|1992]], he completed 145 of 264 passes for 2,092 yards with 41 touchdowns and 10 interceptions. The greatest feat of his career the "Miracle Minute", a historic comeback in a game against the [[Detroit Drive]] on June 19. In that game, he threw two touchdown passes and two 2-point conversions in the final 49 seconds of the game, all to [[Barry Wagner]]. Wagner then got a game-winning safety, completing a comeback from a 32–42 deficit to a 50–49 win. Bennett led the Predators to the [[ArenaBowl VI]], where they were beaten by the Drive.{{cite web| url=https://www.oursportscentral.com/services/releases/top-25-players-in-afl-history-23-ben-bennett/n-4370842 | title=Top 25 Players in AFL History: #23 Ben Bennett | date=March 22, 2012 | access-date=January 27, 2019}} In [[1993 Arena Football League season|1993]], he completed 180 of 340 yards for 2,515 yards with 50 touchdowns and 10 interceptions. In [[1994 Arena Football League season|1994]], he completed 166 of 245 passes for 2,211 yards with 45 touchdowns and 9 interceptions.{{cite web| url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1994/08/06/starting-at-quarterback-the-duke/ | title=Starting At Quarterback . . . The Duke | date=August 6, 1994 | access-date=January 27, 2019}} In [[1995 Arena Football League season|1995]], he completed 91 of 149 passes for 1,111 yards with 20 touchdowns and 7 interceptions. For both the [[1993 Arena Football League season|1993]] and [[1994 Arena Football League season|1994 season]], Bennett was named first-team All-Arena. He would also lead the Predators to a total of three [[ArenaBowl]]s, losing all three. For the [[1996 Arena Football League season|1996 season]], Bennett played for the [[San Jose SaberCats]], completing 26 of 55 passes for 376 yards with 4 touchdowns and 4 interceptions. In [[1997 Arena Football League season|1997]], he played for the [[Oklahoma Wranglers|Portland Forest Dragons]], completing 63 of 124 passes for 792 yards with 14 touchdowns and 6 interceptions. He retired at the end of the year after suffering a neck injury. During his AFL playing career, he made five [[ArenaBowl]] appearances and was inducted into the [[Arena Football Hall of Fame]] on May 24, 2000. He also was inducted into the Predators Ring of Honor. ==Coaching career== In 1998, he was signed as an assistant coach by the [[Milwaukee Mustangs (1994–2001)|Milwaukee Mustangs]]. In December 1998, he was named an assistant coach at [[Duke University]].{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/12/29/sports/transactions-631850.html | title=Transaction | newspaper=The New York Times | date=December 29, 1998 | access-date=January 27, 2019}} In three seasons as a head coach in the af2, Bennett has compiled a record of 36–18 (including playoffs). His win total is the third highest among active coaches and tenth best All-time. Bennett's coaching resume also includes stints as an assistant with the [[Florida Bobcats]] (AFL, 2001), the [[Greensboro Prowlers]] (af2, 2000), and the [[Milwaukee Mustangs (1994–2001)|Milwaukee Mustangs]] (AFL, 1998). Bennett built and led the [[Florida Firecats]] of the af2 to two [[ArenaCup]] championship games during the 2002 and 2004 seasons, winning the 2004 ArenaCup championship. In 2005, he transformed the [[Manchester Wolves]] from a 5–11 team in 2004 into the East Division champion in his first season. He guided the Wolves to a franchise-best 12-win season, finishing 12–5 overall. The team's season also included a 10-game win streak and a trip to the second round of the af2 playoffs. Bennett was to be the head coach for the [[Orlando Fantasy]] during the 2010 season, but he decided that it wasn't a job he was interested in.{{cite news|url=http://blogs.orlandosentinel.com/en_fuego/2010/06/ben-bennett-out-as-coach-of-orlando-lingerie-league-team.html |title=Ben Bennett out as coach of Orlando Lingerie Football League team |author=George Diaz |date=June 8, 2010 |newspaper=Orlando Sentinel |access-date=January 30, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121020204001/http://blogs.orlandosentinel.com/en_fuego/2010/06/ben-bennett-out-as-coach-of-orlando-lingerie-league-team.html |archive-date=October 20, 2012 }} In 2011, he was the [[offensive coordinator]] of the [[Arena Football League]]'s [[New Orleans VooDoo]], but he was dismissed three games into the season. In 2012, he was named [[offensive coordinator]] of the [[Arena Football League]]'s [[Orlando Predators]].{{cite web| url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2012/04/10/orlando-predators-tap-former-qb-ben-bennett-as-offensive-coordinator/ | title=Orlando Predators tap former QB Ben Bennett as offensive coordinator | date=April 10, 2012 | access-date=January 27, 2019}} He was named the head coach of the re-launched [[Orlando Predators (NAL)|Orlando Predators]] in the [[National Arena League]] for the 2020 season.{{cite web |url=http://www.nationalarenaleague.com/news-m/958-orlando-predators-announce-new-ownership-and-the-addition-of-ben-bennett-as-head-coach.html |title=Orlando Predators Announce New Ownership and the Addition of Ben Bennett as Head Coach |website=NAL |date=October 30, 2019 |access-date=October 30, 2019 |archive-date=October 30, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191030224821/http://www.nationalarenaleague.com/news-m/958-orlando-predators-announce-new-ownership-and-the-addition-of-ben-bennett-as-head-coach.html |url-status=dead }} The 2020 season was cancelled due to the onset of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], but Bennett returned for the 2021 season where he led the team to 4–4 record and a playoff spot. He left the Predators after the season.{{cite web |url=https://www.orlandopredatorsfootball.com/news/new-head-coach |title=NEW HEAD COACH |website=Orlando Predators |date=November 18, 2021 |access-date=November 23, 2021 |archive-date=November 23, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211123182424/https://www.orlandopredatorsfootball.com/news/new-head-coach |url-status=dead }} '''Ben Archibald''' (born August 26, 1978) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] [[offensive tackle]]. He was signed by the [[San Francisco 49ers]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2003. He played [[college football]] at [[BYU Cougars football|Brigham Young]].

Archibald also played for the [[Amsterdam Admirals]], [[New Orleans Saints]] and [[Calgary Stampeders]]. He won the [[Grey Cup]] with the [[Calgary Stampeders|Stamps]] in [[96th Grey Cup|2008]] and with [[BC Lions]] in [[99th Grey Cup|2011]].

In [[2010 CFL season|2010]], Archibald won the [[CFL's Most Outstanding Offensive Lineman Award]].

'''Bashir A. Levingston''' ({{IPAc-en|b|ə|ˈ|ʃ|ɑr}} {{respell|bə|SHAR|'}}; born October 2, 1976) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] [[cornerback]] and [[kick returner]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL).

==College career==
After transferring from [[Monterey Peninsula College]], Levingston played [[college football]] at [[Eastern Washington University]], where, as a senior, he earned seven [[All-America]]n honors as a [[kickoff returner|return specialist]].  He was also named first-team All-[[Big Sky Conference]] as a kick returner.  He scored 12 [[touchdowns]] and totaled 1,597 all-purpose yards during his senior year at Eastern Washington.

Livingston also is the leader for [[Division I-AA]] and is fifth on the all-time [[NCAA]] list in [[Punt returner|punt returns]] averaging 20.8 yards.  He broke or tied seven I-AA records including kickoff returns for a touchdown in a game (three) and season (three), kickoff return yards in a game (326), average kickoff returns in a game (65.2), yards in kickoffs and punt returns in game (349) and touchdowns on kickoffs and punt returns in a single game (three) and season (six).

==Professional career==

===NFL and NFL Europa ===
Levingston was originally signed by the [[New York Giants]] in [[1999 NFL season|1999]] and spent two years on the team.  Eventually, he was released from the team and allocated to [[NFL Europa]] with the [[Amsterdam Admirals]] in 2000, where he earned All-NFL Europa honors for his contributions on [[special teams]].

===CFL===
After being cut by the [[Edmonton Eskimos]] during their [[2001 CFL season|2001]] training camp, Levingston caught on with the [[Toronto Argonauts]].  Since being signed in [[2002 CFL season|2002]], Levingston has developed into one of the CFL's best kick returners, earning CFL Special Teams Player of the Week honors ten times in his career to go along with earning [[Canadian Football League East Division|East Division]] All-Star honors in [[2003 CFL season#2003 Eastern All-Stars|2003]] and [[2004 CFL season#2004 Eastern All-Stars|2004]].  Levingston was named the [[John Agro Special Teams Award|CFL's Outstanding Special Teams Player]] and the [[2003 CFL season#2003 Eastern All-Stars|East Division Special Teams Player of the Year]] in [[2003 CFL season|2003]] as well.  In [[2004 CFL season|2004]], Levingston also won a [[92nd Grey Cup|Grey Cup championship]] with the Toronto Argonauts.

On June 28, 2007, in a game against the [[BC Lions]], Levingston broke a CFL record when he returned a missed [[Field goal (football)|field goal]] by [[Paul McCallum (Canadian football)|Paul McCallum]] for a 129-yard touchdown.<ref>{{YouTube|Qouhh-gA08Y}}</ref> That record has since been tied by his then teammate [[Dominique Dorsey]] on August 2, 2007.

On August 30, 2007, Levingston was released by the Argonauts.

On November 4, 2007, Levingston was signed by the [[Montreal Alouettes]].

'''Bart Steven Oates''' (born December 16, 1958) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[center (gridiron football)|center]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[New York Giants]] and [[San Francisco 49ers]].  He played for the Giants from 1985 to 1993 and with the 49ers from 1994 to 1995.  He was a member of the Giants teams that won [[Super Bowl]]s [[Super Bowl XXI|XXI]] and [[Super Bowl XXV|XXV]] and the 49ers team that won [[Super Bowl XXIX]].  He is one of two players (along with [[Sean Landeta]]) to be on both a Super Bowl-winning team and a team that won a championship in the original [[United States Football League]] (USFL).

==College career==
A graduate of [[Albany High School (Albany, Georgia)|Albany High School]] in Georgia,<ref>{{cite web|title=Looking Back 25 Years|url=http://albanygasportshalloffame.org/25years.htm|publisher=Albany Sports Hall of Fame|access-date=October 31, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150201194034/http://albanygasportshalloffame.org/25years.htm|archive-date=February 1, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> Oates played [[college football]] at [[Brigham Young University]] (BYU), originally entering in 1977 before serving an 2-year mission for [[the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints]] in [[Las Vegas, Nevada]] then later joining the Cougars football team.<ref name="BOHOF">[http://www.cougarclub.com/hall_of_fame/index.html Hall of Fame - Bart Oates] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070203160846/http://www.cougarclub.com/hall_of_fame/index.html |date=February 3, 2007 }}, cougarclub.com, accessed January 13, 2007.</ref> Oates earned a BS in accounting from the [[Marriott School of Business]] there in 1985,<ref>{{cite web |last1= |publisher=BYU Marriott School of Business |title=Alumni Directory |url=https://marriottschool.byu.edu/alumnidirectory/ |access-date=September 12, 2019}}</ref> and he was inducted into the BYU athletic Hall of Fame in 1992.<ref name="BOHOF"/>

==Professional career==
The Giants signed Oates in 1985 at the relatively advanced age of 26.  This was because he had initially played three seasons with the [[Philadelphia/Baltimore Stars]] in the [[United States Football League|USFL]] where he won two USFL championships.<ref name="usfl">[http://www.usflonline.readywebsites.com/page/page/2901424.htm Bart Oates interview] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070123061837/http://www.usflonline.readywebsites.com/page/page/2901424.htm |date=January 23, 2007 }}, usflonline.readywebsites.com, accessed January 13, 2007.</ref> Oates has stated that he feels the 1985 [[Philadelphia/Baltimore Stars|Philadelphia Stars]] of the USFL could have beaten the [[1985 Philadelphia Eagles]].<ref name="usfl"/>  Oates won three [[Super Bowls]], two with the Giants in [[Super Bowl XXI|1987]] and [[Super Bowl XXV|1991]], and one with the 49ers in [[Super Bowl XXIX|1995]]. Oates was selected to five [[Pro Bowl]]s during his career and to the [[United Press International|UPI]] All-NFC team three times.  He was extremely durable, starting 125 consecutive games during his Giants career.<ref>[http://www.cougarclub.com/hall_of_fame/oates_b.html Hall of Fame] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927010525/http://www.cougarclub.com/hall_of_fame/oates_b.html |date=September 27, 2007 }}, cougarclub.com, accessed January 13, 2007.</ref>

==Television work==
Oates worked as a [[color analyst]] for NFL games on [[NFL on NBC|NBC]] television in 1996, teaming with either [[Dan Hicks (sportscaster)|Dan Hicks]] or, when Hicks was away on assignment, [[Jim Donovan (sportscaster)|Jim Donovan]]. In 2006, he voiced himself in the ''[[Aqua Teen Hunger Force]]'' episode [[Bart Oates (Aqua Teen Hunger Force episode)|"Bart Oates"]].

==Law career==
Oates attended law school classes during the football off-season and graduated [[magna cum laude]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] degree from [[Seton Hall University School of Law|Seton Hall Law School]] in 1990. He worked in New Jersey with the firms of Ribis Graham and Curtin in Morristown, Raymond Koski and Associates in Fort Lee and the real estate company Gale and Wentworth in Florham Park. His primary focus of practice was real estate and health care. He is a member of the New Jersey State Bar Association.<ref>[http://oberon.lunarpages.com/~stella9/professionals.htm#oates The Stellar Realty Group: Meet Our Professional Team] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070312183732/http://oberon.lunarpages.com/~stella9/professionals.htm#oates |date=March 12, 2007 }}, oberon.lunarpages.com, accessed January 13, 2007.</ref>

==Civic and corporate roles==
Oates was chairman of the New Jersey Hall of Fame, a Hall of Fame for New Jersey residents in a variety of fields ranging from scientists to athletes.<ref>[http://www.njhalloffame.com/boardmembers.htm New Jersey Hall of Fame], njhalloffame, accessed February 27, 2007.</ref> He was selected to be inducted into the New Jersey Hall of Fame Class of 2019.   He also spent time helping out as the line coach at Seton Hall Preparatory School earlier in the decade. He currently serves as the Bishop (lay Pastor) of the Morristown 1st Ward of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, and as the Executive Director of CIT International, promoting partnerships of law enforcement with mental health resources.<ref>[https://www.citinternational.org/page-18826 Bart Oates, Executive Director] at CIT International web site</ref>

==Personal life==
Oates and his wife, Michelle, have three children and reside in [[Harding Township, New Jersey]]. His brother, [[Brad Oates|Brad]], also played offensive line in the NFL for six seasons on five teams.
